title: Connectomics: from C. elegans to the fly and mouse
text:
12_03  CONNECTOMICS: FROM C. ELEGANS TO THE FLY AND THE MOUSE

Cajal drew neurons one at a time, from Golgi-stained sections in which only a small, random fraction of cells were visible (Chapter 4). He could infer the direction of signal flow and the general plan of circuits, but he could never see every connection in a piece of tissue. For a century after him, the wiring diagram of any brain remained mostly unknown. Connectomics is the attempt to fill that gap: to map every neuron and every synapse in a nervous system, or in a defined volume of one, at a resolution where individual synapses can be identified.

The word "connectome" was proposed in 2005, independently by Olaf Sporns, Giulio Tononi and Rolf Kotter, and by Patric Hagmann, by analogy with "genome". At the scale of synapses it means a complete directed graph: nodes are neurons, edges are synaptic connections, and each edge can carry a weight such as the number of synapses between two cells. For an AI reader the analogy is obvious and tempting: the connectome is the architecture and, partially, the weight matrix of a biological network. This section explains how such maps are made, what has been mapped, and why the analogy is useful but incomplete.

THE WORM: 302 NEURONS

The first complete connectome came from the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a worm about a millimetre long that Sydney Brenner chose in the 1960s as a model organism partly because its nervous system was small enough to map completely. The adult hermaphrodite has 302 neurons. John White, Eileen Southgate, Nichol Thomson and Sydney Brenner published the reconstruction in 1986 in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, in a monograph often nicknamed "The Mind of a Worm". The work took years: thousands of serial electron micrographs were photographed, printed, and traced by hand, with neurons followed from section to section and synapses annotated by eye.

The result showed about 7,000 chemical synapses and a few hundred gap junctions (electrical synapses), numbers later refined by re-analysis. Later work by Cook, Emmons and colleagues (published in 2019) produced connectomes for both sexes, including the male, whose nervous system has additional neurons associated with mating.

The worm taught an important lesson early. Having the wiring diagram did not mean understanding the behaviour. Even with all 302 neurons and their connections known, predicting what the worm does requires knowing the signs of synapses (excitatory or inhibitory), their strengths and dynamics, the influence of neuromodulators such as serotonin and neuropeptides that act outside the wired synapses, and the intrinsic properties of each neuron. Cornelia Bargmann and Eve Marder argued in 2013 that the connectome is necessary but not sufficient for understanding a circuit, because neuromodulators can reconfigure the same anatomical wiring into different functional circuits. Marder's work on the crab stomatogastric ganglion, a circuit of around thirty neurons, showed that the same wiring can produce different rhythms depending on modulatory state.

HOW CONNECTOMES ARE MADE

Synapses are tens to hundreds of nanometres across, and the thinnest axons and dendritic spine necks are tens of nanometres wide. Light microscopy, limited by diffraction to roughly 200 nanometres, cannot reliably trace them. Electron microscopy (EM) can. The pipeline has four stages.

1. Sample preparation. Tissue is fixed and stained with heavy metals (such as osmium) that bind membranes, then embedded in resin.

2. Imaging in serial sections. Several approaches exist. Serial section transmission EM cuts the block into ultrathin slices, tens of nanometres thick, collected on tape or grids and imaged. Serial block-face scanning EM, introduced by Winfried Denk and Heinz Horstmann in 2004, images the face of the block, shaves off a thin layer with a diamond knife inside the microscope, and images again. Focused ion beam scanning EM mills away layers with an ion beam, giving very thin, isotropic voxels at the cost of speed. Multibeam scanning microscopes image with many electron beams in parallel to increase throughput.

3. Alignment. Images are stitched within sections and aligned across sections into a 3D volume, correcting distortions from cutting.

4. Segmentation and synapse detection. Every voxel must be assigned to a cell, and synapses identified with their pre- and postsynaptic partners. This is where the scale becomes overwhelming. A cubic millimetre of cortex imaged at a few nanometres per pixel produces on the order of a petabyte of images. Tracing by hand, as was done for the worm, is impossible.

MACHINE LEARNING MAKES CONNECTOMICS POSSIBLE

The bottleneck in connectomics is not microscopy alone but image analysis, and the field's progress depended on deep learning.

Convolutional networks for boundary detection were applied to EM images in the late 2000s and early 2010s, by groups including Sebastian Seung's, to predict which pixels are membranes. Segments were then formed by grouping pixels between boundaries and merging fragments. A notable step was the flood-filling network, reported by Michal Januszewski, Viren Jain and colleagues at Google in Nature Methods in 2018. A flood-filling network is a 3D convolutional network that takes an image patch and the current estimate of one object's mask and iteratively predicts how to extend that object, like a learned flood fill. It reduced errors substantially compared with earlier methods.

Errors still occur, typically merges (two neurons wrongly fused) and splits (one neuron broken into pieces). A single merge error can make two neurons look connected to everything the other connects to. So human proofreading remains essential. Citizen science projects helped: EyeWire, launched from Seung's lab, turned tracing of retinal neurons into an online game, and contributed to a 2014 Nature paper on direction selectivity circuits in the mouse retina. The FlyWire project combined automated segmentation with proofreading by a community of scientists and volunteers.

Synapse detection, the classification of cell types, and identification of subcellular structures also use trained networks. Connectomics is now one of the largest applied computer vision problems in science.

THE FLY

The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster has roughly 100,000 to 150,000 neurons in its adult brain, packed into a volume smaller than a poppy seed, with sophisticated behaviours: flight control, courtship, learning and navigation. In 2020 Louis Scheffer and colleagues at Janelia and Google published in eLife the "hemibrain", a dense connectome of a large part of the central brain, including about 25,000 neurons and millions of synapses. In 2023 Winding, Pedigo, Zlatic, Cardona and colleagues published in Science the connectome of the brain of a Drosophila larva, with about 3,000 neurons.

In 2024 the FlyWire Consortium published, in a package of papers in Nature, a whole-brain connectome of an adult female fly, based on an EM dataset acquired by Zheng, Bock and colleagues. The main paper by Dorkenwald and colleagues reported about 139,000 neurons and around 50 million synaptic connections in its reconstructed wiring diagram, with neurons classified into thousands of cell types. The male adult nervous system, including the ventral nerve cord (the fly's equivalent of the spinal cord), has been mapped in further projects.

What can one do with such a map? One example: Lappalainen, Turaga, Macke and colleagues reported in Nature in 2024 that they built a model of the fly's motion-detection pathway with the connectivity taken from the connectome, trained only the unknown parameters (such as synaptic strengths per cell type and neuron time constants) with gradient descent on a motion-estimation task, and found that the trained model predicted measured neural responses in many cell types. This is an important demonstration of how connectome constraints and deep learning can be combined: the architecture comes from biology, the parameters from optimisation.

THE MOUSE AND THE HUMAN

Mammalian brains are vastly larger. A mouse brain has around 70 million neurons, a human brain around 86 billion. Complete synaptic connectomes of whole mammalian brains are still beyond reach, so the field maps volumes.

The MICrONS project (Machine Intelligence from Cortical Networks), funded by the US Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity (IARPA), aimed explicitly at linking brains and AI. The consortium, including the Allen Institute, Baylor College of Medicine, and Princeton, first recorded calcium activity from neurons in a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex while the mouse viewed visual stimuli, then imaged the same volume with EM and reconstructed it. The result, released openly and described in papers published in Nature in 2025, contains on the order of 200,000 cells and hundreds of millions of synapses, with functional responses for tens of thousands of neurons. This makes it possible to ask whether neurons with similar tuning are more likely to be connected, a direct test of Hebbian ideas (Chapter 7).

In 2024 Alexander Shapson-Coe, Jeff Lichtman, Viren Jain and colleagues published in Science the reconstruction of about one cubic millimetre of human temporal cortex, from tissue removed during epilepsy surgery. The dataset, called H01, is around 1.4 petabytes and includes tens of thousands of cells and roughly 150 million synapses. It revealed rare features such as axons making unusually many synapses onto a single target, which may indicate very strong individual connections.

Mesoscale connectomics, by contrast, maps connections between regions rather than cells, using tracer injections and light microscopy. The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, published in 2014 by Oh and colleagues, is an example. In humans, diffusion MRI tractography (Chapter 10) estimates white matter pathways non-invasively, but it infers fibre directions from water diffusion and has known false positives and negatives; it does not see synapses.

LIMITS OF THE WIRING DIAGRAM

A connectome from EM is a snapshot of a dead brain. It shows where synapses are and their size, which correlates with strength, but not directly their sign in all cases (this can often be inferred from cell type or neurotransmitter predictions), their short-term dynamics, receptor composition, or modulatory state. It omits most neuromodulatory signalling by volume transmission, glial influences, gap junctions in many datasets (they are hard to see in standard EM), and the intrinsic properties of each neuron. It also captures one individual. Comparing fly connectomes from different individuals showed substantial variability in specific connections while cell types and major pathways were conserved.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Architecture versus weights. In deep learning we distinguish architecture (which units connect to which) from weights (learned values). A connectome gives the architecture and a structural proxy for weights. The fly visual system result suggests that architecture plus task-driven optimisation can recover much of a circuit's function, which mirrors an ML lesson: the right inductive bias, such as convolutional weight sharing, makes learning efficient. It also connects to work on "weight-agnostic" networks and lottery-ticket ideas, which suggest that structure alone can carry a surprising amount of function.

2. Biological networks are not layered stacks. Real connectomes have dense recurrence, many reciprocal connections, long-range shortcuts and cell-type-specific motifs. The fly mushroom body, involved in olfactory learning, has an expansion layer, in which a modest number of projection neurons fan out to thousands of Kenyon cells with sparse random-like connections, followed by convergence onto a small number of output neurons, a structure that resembles random feature expansion followed by a learned linear readout. Theoretical work has compared it to kernel methods and to Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, and it has inspired algorithms for similarity search (for example the "fly hashing" algorithm reported by Dasgupta, Stevens and Navlakha in Science in 2017).

3. Deep learning as the enabling tool. Without convolutional networks and flood-filling networks, large connectomes would not exist. The field is a clear case of AI accelerating neuroscience, and it reverses the usual direction of inspiration.

4. Interpretability's connectomics. In mechanistic interpretability, researchers try to reverse-engineer trained networks by mapping "circuits" of features and their connections, a project some practitioners explicitly compare to connectomics. The comparison is instructive. In an artificial network, the full weight matrix is known exactly, yet understanding remains hard. That supports Bargmann and Marder's point: a complete wiring diagram is a starting point for understanding, not the understanding itself.

5. Graph analysis. Connectomes are studied with network science: degree distributions, rich clubs (highly connected hubs connected to each other), motifs, and community structure. Graph neural networks, which learn functions on graphs, are now used both to analyse connectomes and, in some studies, to build models whose computational graph is the connectome itself.

SUMMARY

Connectomics maps nervous systems at synaptic resolution using serial electron microscopy and machine-learning segmentation. From the 302-neuron worm in 1986 to the whole adult fly brain in 2024 and cubic-millimetre volumes of mouse and human cortex, the maps have grown by many orders of magnitude, enabled by deep learning. They give AI researchers real biological architectures to study, and give neuroscientists structural constraints for models. They also teach a humbling lesson that interpretability researchers share: knowing every connection does not, by itself, explain the computation.
